fixes.explanation: Close to the feel of it, but Samuel never says that. He says, "…I am old and gray, and my sons are here with you." Nothing about being weak or tired, friend.
Not quite, friend. The people answer, "You have not cheated us or oppressed us…" and add that he hasn't taken anything from the hand of man. So the answer is False.

That's it. The people reply, "You have not cheated us or oppressed us…" and say he has not taken anything from the hand of man. Samuel then says the LORD and His anointed are witnesses that they have found nothing in his hand, and the people answer, "He is a witness."

Joshua is a good guess, but Samuel doesn't name him here. He says the LORD sent Moses and Aaron, who brought the fathers out of Egypt (1 Samuel 12:8). Joshua is called Moses' assistant in Joshua 1:1. Easy one to mix up, friend.
That's right, baker. Samuel says, "But they forgot the LORD their God…" They were brought out and settled in the land, and then they forgot Him. I think that's a hard turn.

Not this time, friend. Samuel says, "But they forgot the LORD their God…" That comes right after he tells how the fathers were settled in the land. So the answer is True, and in that same verse He sold them into the hand of Sisera the commander of the army of Hazor.
I see why you'd think it, with all those enemies. But Samuel says the LORD delivered them from their enemies on every side, "…and you dwelt securely." Securely is the word, friend.
Right, baker. Samuel says they asked for a king "…even though the LORD your God was your king." They already had the best King there is.

That's kind of you, but Samuel doesn't say it. He says they asked for a king "…even though the LORD your God was your king." Samuel was a prophet of the LORD (1 Samuel 3:20), not the king. The LORD was the one on the throne.

Kish isn't in this part of Samuel's speech, friend. He says they asked for a king "…even though the LORD your God was your king." Kish, Saul's father (1 Samuel 9:1–2), doesn't come into it. The LORD is the King he names.
Around isn't the word, friend. Samuel says, "…then the hand of the LORD will be against you as it was against your fathers." Against is the word. He's warning them.
Yes, baker. The text says, "…all the people greatly feared the LORD and Samuel." Samuel called to the LORD, and on that day the LORD sent thunder and rain. As a result, the people feared.

A nice word, but it's not the one the text uses. It says, "…all the people greatly feared the LORD and Samuel." That came as a result of the thunder and rain the LORD sent that day. The word is feared, friend.

Doubted isn't the word the text uses, friend. The text says, "…all the people greatly feared the LORD and Samuel." The thunder and rain came on the day Samuel called, and as a result the people feared.
Yes, baker. Samuel says the LORD will not abandon His people "…because He was pleased to make you His own." It's about what He chose, not what they earned.
Judging is a good guess, but it isn't the word here. He says, "…far be it from me that I should sin against the LORD by ceasing to pray for you." The word is praying, friend.
Yes, baker. Samuel says, "But if you persist in doing evil, both you and your king will be swept away." Both, not only the king. It's a serious ending.
